# Drafting brief

- Working title: Edge Controller For Aggregate-Current-Limited Electric-Vehicle Charging
- Applicant: Nimo Rotem
- Named inventors: Nimo Rotem
- Starting point: a description of the invention in the inventor's own words
- Prior-art search: none was run. Work with whatever art is in prior_art/, and say plainly in your summary that the art you were given may be incomplete.

## Inventor and filing notes

No priority claim. No federally sponsored research or development. Use broad disclosure-supported claims, a graduated fallback ladder, supported statutory classes, and no means-plus-function language.
=== CONV ===
# Conversation so far

### USER

Here is my invention.

An edge controller manages charging at several electric-vehicle connectors supplied by one electrical branch whose allowable aggregate current is lower than the sum of the connector ratings. Each connector has a controllable contactor, a connector current sensor, a control-pilot interface, and a local connector identifier. A branch current sensor measures total current upstream of the connector contactors. A controller communicates with the connector interfaces and contactors over an isolated local bus.

The controller stores, for each active connector, a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. At each allocation interval, the controller subtracts measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. It first assigns the minimum sustaining current to sessions that can receive it, then distributes remaining current according to energy deficit. The controller sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface and verifies the resulting connector current with the corresponding current sensor.

The branch current sensor is an independent safety input. If measured branch current remains above the branch limit after a reduced pilot command for a verification interval, the controller opens connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until measured branch current is below the branch limit. A contactor is not reclosed until its connector current sensor reports zero, the control-pilot interface reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired. A welded-contactor condition is recorded when connector current remains above a leakage threshold after an open command. The controller then inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates a local fault indicator.

The controller can receive remote schedules and authorizations through a network interface, but it stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in nonvolatile memory. During a network outage it continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process. It does not start a newly connected session unless the local token authorizes that connector and has not expired. Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence and uploaded when communication returns.

A service input permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors by commanding one low-energy pilot transition at a time and confirming the corresponding connector current sensor. The association is stored only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. This prevents a wiring-map error from assigning a current limit to the wrong connector.

The disclosed essential relationship is closed-loop allocation using both per-connector current sensing and independent upstream branch sensing, with staged reduction followed by ordered contactor shedding when branch current does not respond. Offline authorization, welded-contactor isolation, tamper-evident records, and installation mapping are supported additional features.

using exactly the key in the first column. Never invent a citation, never cite a document
that is not listed here, and never describe a reference beyond what its file actually

During a network outage it continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process. It does not start a newly connected session unless the local token authorizes that connector and has not expired. Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence and uploaded when communication returns.

A service input permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors by commanding one low-energy pilot transition at a time and confirming the corresponding connector current sensor. The association is stored only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. This prevents a wiring-map error from assigning a current limit to the wrong connector.

The disclosed essential relationship is closed-loop allocation using both per-connector current sensing and independent upstream branch sensing, with staged reduction followed by ordered contactor shedding when branch current does not respond. Offline authorization, welded-contactor isolation, tamper-evident records, and installation mapping are supported additional features.

1	Sites that install several electric-vehicle charging connectors frequently supply those connectors from a single electrical branch. The branch is protected at an allowable aggregate current, referred to herein as a branch limit, that is commonly lower than the sum of the individual connector ratings. Installing a branch large enough for every connector to draw its full rating at the same time is often impractical, because the cost of the additional service capacity, conductors, and protective devices can exceed the cost of the charging equipment itself.
2	
3	Charging equipment therefore has to share a fixed amount of current among connectors that could collectively demand more. The signalling mechanism ordinarily available for that purpose is the control pilot presented to each vehicle, which advertises a maximum current that the vehicle is permitted to draw. Control-pilot signalling is advisory in nature. The value advertised on the pilot is a command, not a measurement, and the current actually drawn depends on the behaviour of the vehicle receiving it. A vehicle may respond slowly, may respond only in coarse steps, may hold a previous value while its own thermal or state-of-charge logic settles, or may not reduce at all. Control that assumes the commanded value is the delivered value therefore has no way to detect the case in which the branch remains loaded above its limit after a reduction has been ordered, and that case is precisely the one in which the branch protective device is at risk of operating and removing service from every connector on the branch.
4	
5	A further difficulty arises because the branch usually carries loads other than charging. Lighting, building services, and other equipment on the same branch consume part of the allowable aggregate current, and that consumption varies through the day. Allocation that divides the full branch limit among the connectors, without accounting for the varying non-charging portion of the branch load, either overcommits the branch or forces the installer to configure a permanently conservative limit that wastes capacity for most of the day.
6	
7	Sharing schemes that divide available current equally, or in proportion to instantaneous request, also tend to treat every session alike. Where sessions have been served unequally over the course of a shared-capacity period, for example because one session began while the branch was heavily loaded and another began while it was lightly loaded, equal division perpetuates the inequality rather than correcting it.
8	
9	Charging equipment is additionally exposed to conditions that are specific to its power path and its installation. A contactor whose contacts have welded continues to pass current after an open command has been issued, so an allocation scheme that treats an open command as removal of the load will continue to believe that capacity has been released when it has not. Site communication to a remote management system is not continuous, so equipment that depends on a remote authority for both authorization and current limits either stops serving vehicles when the link fails or continues without a governing limit. Multi-connector equipment is also wired by hand, and a transposition between the logical identifier of a connector and the physical contactor and sensor channel that serve it causes a current limit intended for one connector to be applied to another, which defeats the allocation entirely while leaving every individual component apparently functional.
10	
11	There remains a need for charging control that treats the current actually present on the branch and at each connector as the governing quantity, that keeps the branch within its limit even when a vehicle does not honour a reduced pilot command, that allocates the genuinely available portion of the branch limit in a way that corrects accumulated inequality between sessions, and that remains safe and operable when the site link is down, when a contactor has welded, and when the installation wiring map has not been independently confirmed.

3	Overview of the system
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry.
6	
7	The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which is load on the same branch other than the connector stations.
8	
9	A branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of the contactors of the connector stations and measures the total current on the branch conductor 102. The branch current sensor 104 is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured branch current to it.
10	
11	The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the control-pilot interfaces and the contactors of the connector stations, and carries control-pilot status and connector current sensor measurements from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 is isolated between the edge controller 100 and the connector stations.
12	
13	A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.
14	
15	The connector station
16	
17	FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first electric-vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first electric-vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126.
18	
19	The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and the first control-pilot interface 124 reports whether a vehicle is connected. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.
20	
21	Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another.
22	
23	The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.
24	
25	The edge controller
26	
27	FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a nonvolatile memory 132 and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 is further coupled to the branch current sensor 104 of FIG. 1, over which coupling the branch current sensor 104 reports the measured branch current to the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 carries out the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply.
28	
29	The edge controller 100 is further coupled to a local fault indicator 134 and to a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer initiates the association of connector identifiers with physical contactors described below.
30	
31	For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is a stored value that represents the current requested for the session at that connector. The minimum sustaining current is a stored current value that is assigned to the session at that connector before any further distribution of the available charging current is made. The energy-deficit value is a stored value that represents the energy by which the session at that connector has been under-served.
32	
33	Allocation at each allocation interval
34	
35	FIG. 4 shows the process carried out by the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 repeats the allocation portion of the process at each allocation interval. The allocation interval is a recurring period at which the edge controller 100 revises the assigned limits.
36	
37	At an available-charging-current determination step 200, the edge controller 100 subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current that is drawn by the non-charging load 114. The configurable safety reserve is a stored margin that is withheld from allocation, so that the branch is not loaded to its limit.
38	
39	At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to each session at an active connector that can receive it. The minimum sustaining current stored for each such session is assigned to that session before any further distribution of the available charging current is made.
40	
41	At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value.
42	
43	At a limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, the edge controller 100 sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and then verifies the resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector. The allocation is in this way closed loop, using per-connector current sensing together with the independent upstream branch sensing described below.
44	
45	The branch current sensor as an independent safety input
46	
47	The branch current sensor 104 is an independent safety input. It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the available-charging-current determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.
48	
49	At a pilot reduction step 208, the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command to at least one connector of the plurality, that is, an assigned limit lower than the limit previously assigned to that connector, and starts a verification interval. The reduced pilot command is the first stage of the staged sequence.
50	
51	At an ordered contactor shedding step 210, the edge controller 100 determines whether the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command and after the verification interval has elapsed. The verification interval is the period that is allowed to elapse after the reduced pilot command before the measured branch current is re-evaluated. If the measured branch current has fallen below the branch limit within the verification interval, the reduced pilot command has been effective and the edge controller 100 returns to the allocation interval process. If the measured branch current remains above the branch limit at the end of the verification interval, the pilot signalling has not produced the required reduction, and the edge controller 100 opens the connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.
52	
53	The shedding order is a stored value that defines the sequence in which the contactors of the plurality of connector stations are opened. The contactors are opened one at a time, with the measured branch current re-evaluated between openings, and as soon as the measured branch current is below the branch limit no further contactor is opened.
54	
55	The staged sequence of a reduced pilot command, a verification interval, and then ordered interruption of the power path addresses the technical problem set out in the background. A control-pilot command is advisory, and a vehicle that ignores it, responds too slowly, or responds only in coarse steps leaves the branch loaded above its limit. Allocation that works only from commanded values cannot detect that condition at all. By taking the measured branch current from a sensor that is upstream of every connector contactor, and by treating the persistence of an over-limit measurement through a verification interval as the trigger for opening the power path, the edge controller 100 acts at the contactors rather than on the pilot signalling alone.
56	
57	Recovery after shedding
58	
59	At a reclose permissive step 212, the edge controller 100 governs the reclosing of a contactor that has been opened by the ordered contactor shedding step 210. The edge controller 100 does not reclose such a contactor until three conditions are satisfied together: the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.
60	
61	On reclosing, the edge controller 100 resumes the allocation interval process, and the reclosed session takes part in the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202 and the deficit-based distribution step 204 in the ordinary way.
62	
63	Welded-contactor isolation
64	
65	At a welded-contactor isolation step 214, the edge controller 100 records a welded-contactor condition for a connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The leakage threshold is a current magnitude above zero, so that a connector current that has genuinely ceased is distinguished from a connector current that persists after the open command.
66	
67	When the welded-contactor condition has been recorded, the edge controller 100 inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates the local fault indicator 134.
68	
69	Operation during a network outage
70	
71	The edge controller 100 can receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory 132. The signed local authorization token authorizes one or more connectors of the plurality and has an expiry. The last accepted branch limit is the most recent branch limit that the edge controller 100 has accepted.
72	
73	During a network outage the edge controller 100 continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process described above. Charging therefore continues through the outage within the last accepted branch limit. During the outage the last accepted branch limit is the branch limit to which the protection process described above is applied, so that the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command and, when the measured branch current remains above the last accepted branch limit after the reduced pilot command has been sent and the verification interval has elapsed, opens the connector contactors one at a time in the stored shedding order. The edge controller 100 does not start a newly connected session unless the signed local authorization token authorizes that connector and has not expired. No session is started at a connector that the signed local authorization token does not authorize, and no session is started at any connector after the token has expired.
74	
75	Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence held locally by the edge controller 100. The records accumulated during the outage are uploaded when communication returns.
76	
77	Installation mapping through the service input
78	
79	A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. A transposition assigns a current limit intended for one connector to another. Every component continues to function, every sensor continues to report, and the allocation nevertheless governs the wrong power path.
80	
81	The service input 136 permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors. In response to the service input 136, the edge controller 100 commands one low-energy pilot transition at a time, that is, it drives a pilot transition at a single connector, and confirms the corresponding connector current sensor by observing which sensed channel responds to that transition. The transition is a low-energy one, sufficient to produce a distinguishable response at the connector current sensor of the connector that is actually being driven, and the transitions are commanded one at a time so that the responding channel is unambiguous.
82	
83	The association between a connector identifier and a physical contactor is stored only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. If the responding channel is not the channel expected for the commanded connector, or if no channel responds, no association is stored for that connector. The mapping is thus established by measurement on the same sensors that the allocation process later relies upon, so a wiring-map error is found during installation instead of silently misdirecting current limits for the life of the installation.
84	
85	General considerations
86	
87	The allocation process, the branch protection process, the offline authorization behaviour, the welded-contactor isolation, the tamper-evident record sequence, and the installation mapping are described together because they share the sensors and the isolated local bus 106 of a single edge controller 100. They are nevertheless separable. An embodiment may carry out the allocation and branch protection processes without the offline authorization behaviour, without the welded-contactor isolation, without the tamper-evident record sequence, or without the installation mapping described above, and an embodiment may include any combination of those additional features.
88	
89	The branch limit, the configurable safety reserve, the minimum sustaining current, and the shedding order are values stored by the edge controller 100.
90	
91	The terms first and second are used to distinguish one connector station of the plurality from another and do not imply an order of importance or of operation. The system is not limited to two connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each connector station of the plurality. The embodiments described here are illustrative, and a person skilled in the art will recognize that elements described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with elements described in connection with another. The scope of the invention is defined by the claims that follow.
92

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part of this disclosure and show particular embodiments by way of illustration. Other embodiments may be used and structural or logical changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views.

Overview of the system

FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry.

The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which is load on the same branch other than the connector stations.

A branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of the contactors of the connector stations and measures the total current on the branch conductor 102. The branch current sensor 104 is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured branch current to it.

The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the control-pilot interfaces and the contactors of the connector stations, and carries control-pilot status and connector current sensor measurements from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. The isolated local bus 106 is isolated between the edge controller 100 and the connector stations.

A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.

The connector station

FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first electric-vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first electric-vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126.

The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and the first control-pilot interface 124 reports whether a vehicle is connected. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.

Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another.

The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.

The edge controller

FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a nonvolatile memory 132 and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 is further coupled to the branch current sensor 104 of FIG. 1, over which coupling the branch current sensor 104 reports the measured branch current to the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 carries out the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply.

The edge controller 100 is further coupled to a local fault indicator 134 and to a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer initiates the association of connector identifiers with physical contactors described below.

For each active connector of the plurality, the edge controller 100 stores a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. The charging authorization records that the session at that connector is permitted to draw energy. The requested current is a stored value that represents the current requested for the session at that connector. The minimum sustaining current is a stored current value that is assigned to the session at that connector before any further distribution of the available charging current is made. The energy-deficit value is a stored value that represents the energy by which the session at that connector has been under-served.

Allocation at each allocation interval

FIG. 4 shows the process carried out by the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 repeats the allocation portion of the process at each allocation interval. The allocation interval is a recurring period at which the edge controller 100 revises the assigned limits.

At an available-charging-current determination step 200, the edge controller 100 subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. The measured non-charging branch load is the measured portion of the branch current that is drawn by the non-charging load 114. The configurable safety reserve is a stored margin that is withheld from allocation, so that the branch is not loaded to its limit.

At a minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the edge controller 100 first assigns the minimum sustaining current to each session at an active connector that can receive it. The minimum sustaining current stored for each such session is assigned to that session before any further distribution of the available charging current is made.

At a deficit-based distribution step 204, the edge controller 100 distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current, that is, the portion left after the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, according to energy deficit. Sessions with a greater energy-deficit value receive a greater share of the remaining current than sessions with a smaller energy-deficit value.

At a limit transmission and connector current verification step 206, the edge controller 100 sends each assigned limit through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and then verifies the resulting connector current with the connector current sensor of that connector. The allocation is in this way closed loop, using per-connector current sensing together with the independent upstream branch sensing described below.

The branch current sensor as an independent safety input

The branch current sensor 104 is an independent safety input. It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the available-charging-current determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.

At a pilot reduction step 208, the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command to at least one connector of the plurality, that is, an assigned limit lower than the limit previously assigned to that connector, and starts a verification interval. The reduced pilot command is the first stage of the staged sequence.

At an ordered contactor shedding step 210, the edge controller 100 determines whether the measured branch current remains above the branch limit after the reduced pilot command and after the verification interval has elapsed. The verification interval is the period that is allowed to elapse after the reduced pilot command before the measured branch current is re-evaluated. If the measured branch current has fallen below the branch limit within the verification interval, the reduced pilot command has been effective and the edge controller 100 returns to the allocation interval process. If the measured branch current remains above the branch limit at the end of the verification interval, the pilot signalling has not produced the required reduction, and the edge controller 100 opens the connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch limit.

The shedding order is a stored value that defines the sequence in which the contactors of the plurality of connector stations are opened. The contactors are opened one at a time, with the measured branch current re-evaluated between openings, and as soon as the measured branch current is below the branch limit no further contactor is opened.

The staged sequence of a reduced pilot command, a verification interval, and then ordered interruption of the power path addresses the technical problem set out in the background. A control-pilot command is advisory, and a vehicle that ignores it, responds too slowly, or responds only in coarse steps leaves the branch loaded above its limit. Allocation that works only from commanded values cannot detect that condition at all. By taking the measured branch current from a sensor that is upstream of every connector contactor, and by treating the persistence of an over-limit measurement through a verification interval as the trigger for opening the power path, the edge controller 100 acts at the contactors rather than on the pilot signalling alone.

Recovery after shedding

At a reclose permissive step 212, the edge controller 100 governs the reclosing of a contactor that has been opened by the ordered contactor shedding step 210. The edge controller 100 does not reclose such a contactor until three conditions are satisfied together: the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

On reclosing, the edge controller 100 resumes the allocation interval process, and the reclosed session takes part in the assignments made at the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202 and the deficit-based distribution step 204 in the ordinary way.

Welded-contactor isolation

At a welded-contactor isolation step 214, the edge controller 100 records a welded-contactor condition for a connector when the connector current measured by the connector current sensor of that connector remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The leakage threshold is a current magnitude above zero, so that a connector current that has genuinely ceased is distinguished from a connector current that persists after the open command.

When the welded-contactor condition has been recorded, the edge controller 100 inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates the local fault indicator 134.

Operation during a network outage

The edge controller 100 can receive remote schedules and authorizations through the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in the nonvolatile memory 132. The signed local authorization token authorizes one or more connectors of the plurality and has an expiry. The last accepted branch limit is the most recent branch limit that the edge controller 100 has accepted.

During a network outage the edge controller 100 continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process described above. Charging therefore continues through the outage within the last accepted branch limit. During the outage the last accepted branch limit is the branch limit to which the protection process described above is applied, so that the edge controller 100 sends a reduced pilot command and, when the measured branch current remains above the last accepted branch limit after the reduced pilot command has been sent and the verification interval has elapsed, opens the connector contactors one at a time in the stored shedding order. The edge controller 100 does not start a newly connected session unless the signed local authorization token authorizes that connector and has not expired. No session is started at a connector that the signed local authorization token does not authorize, and no session is started at any connector after the token has expired.

Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence held locally by the edge controller 100. The records accumulated during the outage are uploaded when communication returns.

Installation mapping through the service input

A multi-connector installation is wired by hand, and the identifier a connector is given in configuration must correspond to the physical contactor and the physical current sensor channel that serve that connector. A transposition assigns a current limit intended for one connector to another. Every component continues to function, every sensor continues to report, and the allocation nevertheless governs the wrong power path.

The service input 136 permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors. In response to the service input 136, the edge controller 100 commands one low-energy pilot transition at a time, that is, it drives a pilot transition at a single connector, and confirms the corresponding connector current sensor by observing which sensed channel responds to that transition. The transition is a low-energy one, sufficient to produce a distinguishable response at the connector current sensor of the connector that is actually being driven, and the transitions are commanded one at a time so that the responding channel is unambiguous.

The association between a connector identifier and a physical contactor is stored only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector. If the responding channel is not the channel expected for the commanded connector, or if no channel responds, no association is stored for that connector. The mapping is thus established by measurement on the same sensors that the allocation process later relies upon, so a wiring-map error is found during installation instead of silently misdirecting current limits for the life of the installation.

General considerations

The allocation process, the branch protection process, the offline authorization behaviour, the welded-contactor isolation, the tamper-evident record sequence, and the installation mapping are described together because they share the sensors and the isolated local bus 106 of a single edge controller 100. They are nevertheless separable. An embodiment may carry out the allocation and branch protection processes without the offline authorization behaviour, without the welded-contactor isolation, without the tamper-evident record sequence, or without the installation mapping described above, and an embodiment may include any combination of those additional features.

The branch limit, the configurable safety reserve, the minimum sustaining current, and the shedding order are values stored by the edge controller 100.

The terms first and second are used to distinguish one connector station of the plurality from another and do not imply an order of importance or of operation. The system is not limited to two connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each connector station of the plurality. The embodiments described here are illustrative, and a person skilled in the art will recognize that elements described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with elements described in connection with another. The scope of the invention is defined by the claims that follow.

An edge controller manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by one electrical branch whose allowable aggregate current, called the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors. Each connector of the plurality forms part of a connector station that further comprises a contactor, a connector current sensor, a control-pilot interface, and a local connector identifier. A branch current sensor measures total current on the branch upstream of the connector contactors. The controller communicates with the connector interfaces and the contactors over an isolated local bus.

The controller stores, for each active connector, a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current, and an energy-deficit value. At each allocation interval the controller subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch limit to obtain an available charging current. It first assigns the minimum sustaining current to the sessions that can receive it, and then distributes the remaining portion of the available charging current according to energy deficit, so that a session that has been served less is preferred over a session that has been served more. Each assigned limit is sent through the control-pilot interface of the corresponding connector, and the resulting connector current is then verified with the connector current sensor of that same connector. Allocation is therefore closed loop, using per-connector current sensing together with independent upstream branch sensing.

The branch current sensor is an independent safety input: beyond supplying the branch measurement used in the allocation arithmetic, it governs a protection process that acts on the power path. When measured branch current remains above the branch limit after a reduced pilot command has been issued and a verification interval has elapsed, the controller opens connector contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order until measured branch current is below the branch limit.

Recovery is likewise conditioned on measurement. A contactor that has been opened by the shedding sequence is not reclosed until the connector current sensor of that connector reports zero current, the control-pilot interface of that connector reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired.

A welded-contactor condition is recorded when connector current remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector. The controller then inhibits the other contactors on the same branch and operates a local fault indicator.

The controller can receive remote schedules and authorizations through a network interface, and also stores a signed local authorization token and the last accepted branch limit in nonvolatile memory. During a network outage the controller continues already authorized sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and the independent branch-current safety process, and does not start a newly connected session unless the local token authorizes that connector and has not expired. Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence and uploaded when communication returns.

A service input permits an installer to associate connector identifiers with physical contactors by commanding one low-energy pilot transition at a time and confirming the corresponding connector current sensor. The association is stored only after the sensed channel agrees with the commanded connector, which prevents a wiring-map error from assigning a current limit to the wrong connector.

Embodiments include a charging control system and a method of controlling charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch.

Sites that install several electric-vehicle charging connectors frequently supply those connectors from a single electrical branch. The branch is protected at an allowable aggregate current, referred to herein as a branch limit, that is commonly lower than the sum of the individual connector ratings. Installing a branch large enough for every connector to draw its full rating at the same time is often impractical, because the cost of the additional service capacity, conductors, and protective devices can exceed the cost of the charging equipment itself.

Charging equipment therefore has to share a fixed amount of current among connectors that could collectively demand more. The signalling mechanism ordinarily available for that purpose is the control pilot presented to each vehicle, which advertises a maximum current that the vehicle is permitted to draw. Control-pilot signalling is advisory in nature. The value advertised on the pilot is a command, not a measurement, and the current actually drawn depends on the behaviour of the vehicle receiving it. A vehicle may respond slowly, may respond only in coarse steps, may hold a previous value while its own thermal or state-of-charge logic settles, or may not reduce at all. Control that assumes the commanded value is the delivered value therefore has no way to detect the case in which the branch remains loaded above its limit after a reduction has been ordered, and that case is precisely the one in which the branch protective device is at risk of operating and removing service from every connector on the branch.

A further difficulty arises because the branch usually carries loads other than charging. Lighting, building services, and other equipment on the same branch consume part of the allowable aggregate current, and that consumption varies through the day. Allocation that divides the full branch limit among the connectors, without accounting for the varying non-charging portion of the branch load, either overcommits the branch or forces the installer to configure a permanently conservative limit that wastes capacity for most of the day.

Sharing schemes that divide available current equally, or in proportion to instantaneous request, also tend to treat every session alike. Where sessions have been served unequally over the course of a shared-capacity period, for example because one session began while the branch was heavily loaded and another began while it was lightly loaded, equal division perpetuates the inequality rather than correcting it.

Charging equipment is additionally exposed to conditions that are specific to its power path and its installation. A contactor whose contacts have welded continues to pass current after an open command has been issued, so an allocation scheme that treats an open command as removal of the load will continue to believe that capacity has been released when it has not. Site communication to a remote management system is not continuous, so equipment that depends on a remote authority for both authorization and current limits either stops serving vehicles when the link fails or continues without a governing limit. Multi-connector equipment is also wired by hand, and a transposition between the logical identifier of a connector and the physical contactor and sensor channel that serve it causes a current limit intended for one connector to be applied to another, which defeats the allocation entirely while leaving every individual component apparently functional.

There remains a need for charging control that treats the current actually present on the branch and at each connector as the governing quantity, that keeps the branch within its limit even when a vehicle does not honour a reduced pilot command, that allocates the genuinely available portion of the branch limit in a way that corrects accumulated inequality between sessions, and that remains safe and operable when the site link is down, when a contactor has welded, and when the installation wiring map has not been independently confirmed.

Control that assumes the commanded value is the delivered value therefore has no way to detect the case in which the branch remains loaded above its limit after a reduction has been ordered, and that case is precisely the one in which the branch protective device is at risk of operating and removing service from every connector on the branch.

A further difficulty arises because the branch usually carries loads other than charging. Lighting, building services, and other equipment on the same branch consume part of the allowable aggregate current, and that consumption varies through the day. Allocation that divides the full branch limit among the connectors, without accounting for the varying non-charging portion of the branch load, either overcommits the branch or forces the installer to configure a permanently conservative limit that wastes capacity for most of the day.

Sharing schemes that divide available current equally, or in proportion to instantaneous request, also tend to treat every session alike. Where sessions have been served unequally over the course of a shared-capacity period, for example because one session began while the branch was heavily loaded and another began while it was lightly loaded, equal division perpetuates the inequality rather than correcting it.

Charging equipment is additionally exposed to conditions that are specific to its power path and its installation. A contactor whose contacts have welded continues to pass current after an open command has been issued, so an allocation scheme that treats an open command as removal of the load will continue to believe that capacity has been released when it has not. Site communication to a remote management system is not continuous, so equipment that depends on a remote authority for both authorization and current limits either stops serving vehicles when the link fails or continues without a governing limit. Multi-connector equipment is also wired by hand, and a transposition between the logical identifier of a connector and the physical contactor and sensor channel that serve it causes a current limit intended for one connector to be applied to another, which defeats the allocation entirely while leaving every individual component apparently functional.

There remains a need for charging control that treats the current actually present on the branch and at each connector as the governing quantity, that keeps the branch within its limit even when a vehicle does not honour a reduced pilot command, that allocates the genuinely available portion of the branch limit in a way that corrects accumulated inequality between sessions, and that remains safe and operable when the site link is down, when a contactor has welded, and when the installation wiring map has not been independently confirmed.

5:FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry.
17:FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first electric-vehicle connector 126. 27:FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. 35:FIG. 4 shows the process carried out by the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 repeats the allocation portion of the process at each allocation interval. The allocation interval is a recurring period at which the edge controller 100 revises the assigned limits.

It is not merely a further term in the allocation arithmetic of the available-charging-current determination step 200: it governs a protection process that acts on the power path and that does not depend on the cooperation of any vehicle. The protection process is described with continued reference to FIG. 4.

reasoning: The three Background deletions were genuine source-fidelity defects, not false positives. The disclosure says only that the branch's allowable aggregate current is lower than the sum of the connector ratings and that the controller subtracts measured non-charging branch load. It says nothing about relative installation cost, nothing about what a vehicle's internal logic is doing when it holds a previous pilot value, and nothing about lighting or building services. With an empty prior-art set there is also no reference to attribute those characterisations to. I cut them rather than re-source them, because none is load-bearing: the Background still sets up all four problems the claims answer, namely that the pilot is a command and not a measurement, that the non-charging portion of the branch load varies, that a welded contactor keeps passing current after an open command, and that a wiring-map transposition misdirects a limit while every component still appears to work.

I did not touch the Summary, Detailed Description, claims, numerals or the other three briefs. The reviewer's own ledger confirmed every limitation of claims 1 to 14 traces to an exact passage of the disclosure and that both findings from the prior QA round were already fixed. Rewriting good text to make a check look busier would have destroyed that record.

Claim 1 still carries the whole disclosed essential relationship and nothing more: per-connector current sensing and an independent upstream branch current sensor above the contactors, allocation that subtracts measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve before assigning minimum sustaining current and then distributing the remainder by energy deficit, each assigned limit sent on the control pilot and then verified at the connector current sensor, and the staged fallback of reduced pilot command, verification interval, then opening contactors one at a time in a stored shedding order. The feature doing the real work is the split between the command path and the measurement path: the reduced pilot command is treated as advisory, and the persistence of an over-limit branch measurement through the verification interval is what authorises action on the power path.

I deliberately kept out of claim 1 everything the disclosure calls a supported additional feature, so each has somewhere to retreat to: the three-condition reclose permissive (claims 2 and 10), welded-contactor recording above a leakage threshold and the isolation plus local fault indicator that follows (claims 3, 4 and 11), the offline behaviour built on a signed local token and last accepted branch limit in nonvolatile memory (claims 5, 6, 7, 12 and 13), and the installation mapping by one low-energy pilot transition at a time (claims 8 and 14). The local connector identifier likewise stays out of claim 1 and appears only where the mapping claims need it.

Because prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, there is no reference to write around and no citation to place, so the Background carries no [REF:...] marker. That is a real limit on this draft rather than a drafting choice, and it is why the claim shape rests on what the disclosure calls the essential relationship rather than on distance from any cited document.

On FIG. 4 I applied the rule that drawings follow the invention rather than the reverse. The merged return web was drawing convenience, not disclosed structure, so simplifying it costs the application nothing; had the problem instead been that a rendered sheet showed something the text does not support, the correct move would have been to regenerate the sheet, never to widen the text to match it.

On FIG. 4 I applied the rule that drawings follow the invention rather than the reverse. The merged return web was drawing convenience, not disclosed structure, so simplifying it costs the application nothing; had the problem instead been that a rendered sheet showed something the text does not support, the correct move would have been to regenerate the sheet, never to widen the text to match it.

figures/FIG-4.md: replaced the three merging return lines with a single return path from the reclose permissive step 212, running below both columns clear of every rectangle and ending with one arrowhead at the left side of the available-charging-current determination step 200. The art supplied to this application may therefore be incomplete, and the independent claims are not supported by any comparison against searched art. What claim 1 does instead is recite, in the invention's own vocabulary, the relationship the disclosure identifies as essential and that a command-only allocation scheme cannot perform: allocation closed around two independent measurements, per-connector current sensing at each connector station and branch current sensing upstream of every connector contactor, with a reduced pilot command that must be proved by measurement through a verification interval before ordered one-at-a-time contactor shedding follows. The specification states the technical problem this solves before it is needed, in the Background and again in the Detailed Description passage on the staged sequence: a control-pilot value is a command rather than a measurement, so a vehicle that ignores it, answers slowly, or answers only in coarse steps leaves the branch above its limit, and a controller working only from commanded values cannot detect that condition at all. input.summary: Both listed items trace to one defect in figures/FIG-2.md, and only that file changed. The endpoint rule and the matching geometry bullet for the isolated local bus 106 described the target region as lying both below the enclosing rectangle of the first connector station 110 and to the left of it, which names two horizontal regions that cannot both hold, and left unstated the one constraint that decides the leader, namely that the terminal point sit outside the rectangle's horizontal span. Both sentences now say that in positional terms. The geometry bullet states that a left portion of the bus line lies entirely to the left of the left side of the enclosing rectangle, at horizontal positions smaller than the horizontal position of that left side, and the endpoint sentence directs the leader to a point on that line whose horizontal position lies to the left of the left side of the enclosing rectangle, outside the horizontal span of that rectangle. The added wording pushed the brief over the 2800-character ceiling, so I recovered the space inside the same file without touching any disclosed relationship: the shading phrase left the view line, the redundant identifying sentences for the first electric-vehicle connector 126 and the first control-pilot interface 124 fold into their bullets, the bus branch clause names the three elements it reaches rather than repeating underside for each, and the series note now uses a semicolon. The brief stands at 2798 characters and still carries exactly 102, 106, 110, 120, 122, 124 and 126. Nothing else in the workspace moved. The claims, the detailed description, the drawing descriptions, draft/numerals.md and the briefs for FIG. 1, FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 are unchanged, so the 23 numerals remain defined once each and listed on one sheet each, the bus data flow described in the detailed description still matches the FIG. 2 branching, no sheet lists more than eight numerals, and no sectional view exists to require a cutting-plane line or section designation. As input/brief.md records, no prior-art search was run and prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the art available to this application may be incomplete.
reasoning: The defect was in how the drawing specification named a region, not in the invention, so the repair stayed inside the figure brief. The isolated local bus in FIG. 2 runs beneath the enclosing rectangle before rising into it, so below the rectangle and to the left of the rectangle pick out different horizontal ranges; joining them with both made the instruction unsatisfiable on its face and let the earlier terminal point at an x inside the rectangle span read as compliant. Stating the constraint as a horizontal position to the left of the rectangle's left side removes the conflict, because that is the single condition the inspection measures.

I kept the constraint expressed as a broad region rather than a coordinate. Any point on the left run of the bus qualifies, so the leader has room to avoid crossings without a midpoint, depth, or fractional-position modifier, none of which the disclosure supports.

The geometry bullet and the endpoint sentence had to be corrected together. Leaving the bullet saying clear of the rectangle both below it and to the left of it would have left the same contradiction one layer down, where the renderer resolves what the line looks like before any leader is placed.

Character budget forced choices, and I spent it on wording rather than substance. What went was duplication: the phrase about no shading, two sentences that restated a rectangle's identity after already placing it, and the repetition of underside three times in the bus branch clause. What stayed was every disclosed relationship: the contactor and the connector current sensor both straddling the same power path between the branch conductor and the connector, the pilot interface tied to the connector, and the bus reaching the pilot interface, the contactor and the sensor, which is what the detailed description says the bus carries in both directions.

The note that the two power-path devices lie in series and that their order along the path is a drawing convention stayed, and the left one and right one wording stayed. The disclosure gives no order for those devices, so the sheet must not be readable as disclosing one, and naming them by side rather than by ordinal keeps the renderer from resolving the sequence in either direction on its own.

Nothing in draft/ was touched. The reviewer's ledger closed on the claims, description, abstract and numeral table, and the only reported source-fidelity blocker was this same FIG. 2 wording, so editing the specification text would have risked a regression to cure a defect that never lived there.

content:
The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the control-pilot interfaces and the contactors of the connector stations, and carries control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. Each connector current sensor is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured connector current to it. In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part of this disclosure and show particular embodiments by way of illustration. Other embodiments may be used and structural or logical changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views.

Overview of the system

FIG. 1 shows a charging control system in which an edge controller 100 manages charging at a plurality of electric-vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 supplies the plurality of connectors. The allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, referred to in this description as the branch limit, is lower than the sum of the ratings of the connectors that the branch conductor 102 supplies. The branch limit is a stored value that corresponds to the aggregate current the branch is permitted to carry.

The branch conductor 102 supplies a first connector station 110 and a second connector station 112. Two connector stations are shown for clarity of illustration. The system accommodates a larger plurality of connector stations, and the description of the first connector station 110 applies to each further connector station of the plurality. The branch conductor 102 also supplies a non-charging load 114, which is load on the same branch other than the connector stations.

A branch current sensor 104 is located upstream of the contactors of the connector stations and measures the total current on the branch conductor 102. The branch current sensor 104 is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured branch current to it.

The edge controller 100 communicates with the connector stations over an isolated local bus 106. The isolated local bus 106 carries assigned current limits and contactor commands from the edge controller 100 to the control-pilot interfaces and the contactors of the connector stations, and carries control-pilot status from the connector stations to the edge controller 100. Each connector current sensor is coupled to the edge controller 100 and reports the measured connector current to it. The isolated local bus 106 is isolated between the edge controller 100 and the connector stations.

A network interface 108 connects the edge controller 100 to a remote management system. As described below, the network interface 108 conveys remote schedules and authorizations to the edge controller 100 and conveys uploaded meter records from the edge controller 100, but the safety behaviour of the system does not depend on the availability of the network interface 108.

The connector station

FIG. 2 shows the first connector station 110 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The first connector station 110 comprises a first contactor 120, a first connector current sensor 122, a first control-pilot interface 124, and a first electric-vehicle connector 126. The first contactor 120 is connected in the power path between the branch conductor 102 and the first electric-vehicle connector 126 and, when closed, permits current to flow from the branch conductor 102 to a vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126. The first connector current sensor 122 measures the connector current flowing in that power path, that is, the current actually drawn by the vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126.

The first control-pilot interface 124 presents a control-pilot signal to the vehicle coupled to the first electric-vehicle connector 126. The control-pilot signal advertises a maximum current, called here the assigned limit, that the vehicle is permitted to draw, and the first control-pilot interface 124 reports whether a vehicle is connected. The first control-pilot interface 124 therefore serves both as the command path by which an assigned limit reaches the vehicle and as a status path by which the presence of a connected vehicle is reported to the edge controller 100.

Each connector station of the plurality further has a local connector identifier. The local connector identifier is a stored value that distinguishes one connector of the plurality from another.

The distinction between the first control-pilot interface 124 and the first connector current sensor 122 is used throughout this description. The first control-pilot interface 124 carries a command. The first connector current sensor 122 carries a measurement. The edge controller 100 does not treat the assigned limit sent through the first control-pilot interface 124 as evidence of the current that the connector is drawing. It obtains that evidence from the first connector current sensor 122.

The edge controller

FIG. 3 shows the edge controller 100 of FIG. 1 in greater detail. The edge controller 100 comprises a nonvolatile memory 132 and is coupled to the isolated local bus 106 and to the network interface 108. The edge controller 100 is further coupled to the branch current sensor 104 of FIG. 1, over which coupling the branch current sensor 104 reports the measured branch current to the edge controller 100. The edge controller 100 carries out the allocation and protection processes described below. The nonvolatile memory 132 retains stored values across loss of supply.

The edge controller 100 is further coupled to a local fault indicator 134 and to a service input 136. The local fault indicator 134 provides an indication at the equipment itself, independently of the network interface 108. The service input 136 is an input by which an installer initiates the association of connector identifiers with physical contactors described below.

# FIG. 4

View: process flow diagram of the allocation interval and of the staged branch-protection sequence, in plain line work with no shading. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the filing margins. No text or lettering is drawn by the geometry; the numerals below are applied afterward. Each step is a plain rectangle, and the steps are joined by lines carrying a single arrowhead that shows the direction of flow.

Geometry:

- Four rectangles are stacked in a column in the left half of the drawing area. From the top downward these are the available-charging-current determination step 200, the minimum sustaining current assignment step 202, the deficit-based distribution step 204, and the limit transmission and connector current verification step 206. A line with a downward arrowhead joins each of these rectangles to the one below it.
- Three rectangles are stacked in a column in the right half of the drawing area. From the top downward these are the pilot reduction step 208, the ordered contactor shedding step 210, and the reclose permissive step 212. Lines with downward arrowheads join 208 to 210 and 210 to 212.
- A horizontal line runs from the right side of the limit transmission and connector current verification step 206 to the left side of the pilot reduction step 208, with an arrowhead at that left side.
- A rectangle stands in the lower right region of the drawing area, below and to the right of the ordered contactor shedding step 210. This rectangle is the welded-contactor isolation step 214. A line runs from the right side of the ordered contactor shedding step 210 to the top side of the welded-contactor isolation step 214, with an arrowhead at that top side.
- A return line leaves the bottom side of the reclose permissive step 212, runs downward and then to the left below both columns and clear of every rectangle, turns upward along the left part of the drawing area, and ends with an arrowhead at the left side of the available-charging-current determination step 200, so that the process returns to the allocation interval.
